questions.q: Compared with hash(key) mod N, what problem does consistent hashing primarily solve?
options: It eliminates hash collisions entirely by spreading keys over a wider keyspace
It guarantees every node stores exactly the same number of keys at all times
It keeps key remapping small when nodes are added or removed
It removes the need for replication by storing keys on multiple nodes
questions.explanation: Modulo hashing remaps almost every key when N changes, whereas the ring only reassigns the arc belonging to the joining or leaving node, roughly 1/N of keys.

questions.q: On a consistent hash ring, which node owns a given key?
options: The first node found moving clockwise from the key's hash position
The node whose hash value is numerically closest on either side of the key
The node currently holding the fewest keys, to keep load balanced
A node chosen by taking the key's hash modulo the current node count
questions.explanation: Ownership is defined by successor lookup: hash the key onto the ring and walk clockwise to the next node position. This rule is stable, so it depends only on nearby positions, not on N.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of virtual nodes (vnodes)?
options: They add redundancy so each key survives the loss of one physical machine
They smooth load by giving each physical node many ring positions
They reduce memory usage by letting several machines share one ring position
They speed up lookups by shrinking the number of ring positions searched
questions.explanation: Many small random arcs per server average out, so each machine ends up with close to its fair share instead of whatever a few random placements happened to give it.

questions.q: A node is removed from the ring. Which keys must move?
options: All keys, because the ring's total capacity has changed
Keys on every node, redistributed evenly to rebalance the whole ring
Only keys whose hash exactly equals the departed node's position
Only the departed node's keys, which shift to the next node clockwise
questions.explanation: Removing a position merges its arc into the successor's arc, so only the keys that node owned change hands. Every other key's successor is unchanged.

questions.q: With N evenly loaded nodes, roughly what fraction of keys moves when one node leaves?
options: About 1/N of all keys
About half of all keys
About (N-1)/N of all keys
Essentially none of the keys
questions.explanation: Each node owns about 1/N of the keyspace, and only its share is reassigned. That minimal-disruption property is the whole point compared with modulo hashing.

questions.q: Which component most commonly uses consistent hashing?
options: A write-ahead log assigning sequence numbers to transactions
A CPU scheduler assigning threads to cores on one machine
A distributed cache routing keys across a server fleet
A compiler allocating registers across basic blocks
questions.explanation: Caches like memcached and Dynamo-style stores need stateless key-to-server routing that survives membership churn without invalidating the whole cache, which is exactly what the ring provides.

questions.q: Without virtual nodes and with only a few physical nodes, what tends to go wrong?
options: Hash collisions between node identifiers make key ownership ambiguous on the ring
Random placement can leave some nodes owning far larger arcs than others
Lookup time grows linearly because the whole ring must be scanned
Keys become unreachable in the gaps between distant node positions
questions.explanation: A handful of random positions rarely divides the circle evenly, so arc sizes vary widely and some servers get several times the load of others. Keys are never lost, just unevenly spread.

questions.q: Which data structure enables efficient successor lookup on the ring?
options: A bloom filter over the identifiers of nodes currently in the ring
A queue of nodes ordered by the time each joined the cluster
A hash table mapping every possible key directly to its owner
A sorted array of node positions searched with binary search
questions.explanation: Keeping positions sorted lets a binary search find the first position greater than the key's hash in O(log V), wrapping to index zero at the end. A hash table cannot answer successor queries.

questions.q: You add one node to a consistent-hashed cache cluster. What happens to hit rate right away?
options: A small dip: only keys in the arcs the new node claims now miss
A total collapse, since every key now maps to a different server
No change, because existing entries are copied before the node joins
A rise, because the extra capacity immediately serves more requests
questions.explanation: Only the keys whose successor became the new empty node miss and get refetched; everything else still routes to a server that already holds it, so the dip is roughly 1/N.

questions.q: Your fleet has one server with double the RAM and CPU. How do you give it proportionally more load?
options: Hash its identifier with a faster function so it wins more ties
Place it at position zero on the ring, which owns the largest arc
Lower its replication factor so it spends less effort on copies
Assign it more virtual nodes than the smaller machines
questions.explanation: Load is proportional to total arc length, which is proportional to vnode count, so giving it twice as many tokens yields roughly twice the share. This is standard weighted consistent hashing.

questions.q: In Dynamo-style stores, how is replication layered onto the ring?
options: Each key is written to the N nodes whose identifiers share a hash prefix
Replicas are chosen randomly per write and recorded in a directory service
A key lives on its owner plus the next distinct successors clockwise
The ring is duplicated N times, each copy holding one full replica
questions.explanation: The coordinator plus the following N-1 distinct physical nodes form the preference list, so replica placement needs no extra metadata. Skipping duplicates keeps copies on different machines.

questions.q: A node fails abruptly (no virtual nodes in use). Where does its load go?
options: It rebalances evenly across every surviving node in the cluster
Its whole arc shifts onto its immediate clockwise successor
It moves to whichever node has the most free capacity at that moment
Its keys stay unavailable until an operator rebuilds the ring
questions.explanation: With one position per node, the dead node's entire arc merges into the next node's, so a single neighbor inherits all of it and can be pushed into overload.

questions.q: Why do virtual nodes make failure recovery smoother?
options: A failed node's load spreads across many successors instead of one neighbor
Virtual nodes hold complete copies of the data, so nothing ever needs to move at all
They shrink the keyspace, so there is simply less data to transfer
They pause the failed node's tokens until it rejoins the ring
questions.explanation: Each of the node's hundreds of arcs has a different clockwise successor, so recovery load and data transfer parallelize across the fleet instead of hammering one machine.

questions.q: Consistent hashing vs a central placement directory for shards: what is the core tradeoff?
options: A directory cannot support adding new shards without cluster downtime
Hashing avoids per-key metadata; a directory allows arbitrary placement but must stay available
A directory is always faster because it avoids computing a hash per request
Hashing allows fine-grained manual placement while a directory does not
questions.explanation: The ring computes placement from the key alone, so there is nothing to store or keep highly available, but you lose the ability to relocate an individual hot key the way a directory allows.

questions.q: A cache client library does consistent hashing client-side. What goes wrong during a rolling membership change?
options: Every cache server must fully restart whenever any single client updates its member list
The hash function's seed must rotate on every membership change
Ring lookups degrade to O(N) while any two clients disagree
Clients with stale views route some keys to different servers, causing misses
questions.explanation: Ring correctness depends on all clients sharing one membership view; while views differ, the same key resolves to different servers, causing misses and duplicate cached copies.

questions.q: Jump consistent hash is a ring alternative. What is its key limitation?
options: It relocates far more keys than a ring does whenever the bucket count changes at all
Its lookup cost grows linearly with the number of buckets
It addresses numbered buckets only, so removing an arbitrary node is awkward
It cannot achieve an even distribution of keys across buckets
questions.explanation: Jump hash maps a key to an integer in [0, n), so it handles growing or shrinking the count at the tail but has no notion of deleting bucket 3 from the middle. Its balance and O(log n) speed are excellent.

questions.q: 10 nodes, 100 virtual nodes each; one node dies. Roughly how does load shift?
options: A single clockwise neighbor absorbs the entire share, roughly doubling its load
Only the two adjacent nodes gain load, each taking about half the arcs
No survivor gains load because the dead node's virtual nodes stay parked
Each survivor gains roughly one-ninth more load as the arcs scatter evenly
questions.explanation: The 100 orphaned arcs have successors spread randomly over the 9 survivors, so each absorbs about 1/9 of the dead node's share, raising its own load by roughly 11%.

questions.q: You raise vnodes per node from 8 to 512. What is the real tradeoff?
options: Smoother balance, but bigger ring metadata and more fragmented data transfers
Strictly faster ring lookups, at the price of a noticeably less uniform key distribution
Lower memory use, but many more keys move on every membership change
Stronger consistency, but extra coordination required on every write
questions.explanation: More tokens tighten load variance, but the ring table grows 64x for every client to hold and gossip, and rebalancing becomes many tiny scattered range transfers instead of few sequential ones.

questions.q: A single celebrity key overloads its owner. Why don't more vnodes help, and what does?
options: Vnodes only apply to writes; enabling read-through caching fixes it
Hashing is deterministic per key; rotating the hash function hourly fixes it
One key always maps to one owner; replicate or split that hot key instead
Vnodes fail under high QPS; widening the ring's bit space spreads the key
questions.explanation: Vnodes balance many keys, but a single key has one hash and therefore one owner no matter how finely the ring is cut. Extra replicas for reads, or salted sub-keys, actually distribute the traffic.

questions.q: Scaling a consistent-hashed cache from 20 to 40 nodes with minimal client-visible misses: best plan?
options: Add all 20 new nodes simultaneously so the ring only has to change a single time
Add nodes gradually, warming each one's arcs before it serves traffic
Flush the entire cache first so every node starts from a clean state
Double every key's TTL so entries survive until the ring stabilizes
questions.explanation: Incremental joins keep each miss wave small, and prefilling a new node's arcs before it takes traffic means the origin never sees a thundering herd. Adding all 20 at once invalidates half the keyspace instantly.
